import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def top_share(M):            # share of squared Frobenius norm in the top singular direction (rows = units)
    s = np.linalg.svd(M, compute_uv=False); return (s[0]**2/np.sum(s**2))
dirs_g, dirs_d = {}, {}
for L in (10,11,12):
    Wg = load_original(f'model.layers.{L}.mlp.gate_proj.weight').numpy()
    Wu = load_original(f'model.layers.{L}.mlp.up_proj.weight').numpy()
    Wd = load_original(f'model.layers.{L}.mlp.down_proj.weight').numpy()
    _,_,Vt = np.linalg.svd(Wu, full_matrices=False); v0=Vt[0]
    grp = E2rows[L]; s = np.sign(Wu[grp]@v0)
    G = Wg[grp]; Dc = Wd[:, grp].T                     # n x 1152 each
    rnd = [np.setdiff1d(rng.choice(6912, len(grp), replace=False), grp) for _ in range(30)]
    tg = top_share(G); tg_r = np.mean([top_share(Wg[r]) for r in rnd])
    td = top_share(Dc); td_r = np.mean([top_share(Wd[:, r].T) for r in rnd])
    # signed coherence of down columns: |sum s_i d_i| vs sqrt(sum |d_i|^2)
    coh_s = np.linalg.norm((s[:,None]*Dc).sum(0))/np.sqrt((Dc**2).sum()); coh_u = np.linalg.norm(Dc.sum(0))/np.sqrt((Dc**2).sum())
    _,_,Vg = np.linalg.svd(G, full_matrices=False); _,_,Vd = np.linalg.svd(Dc, full_matrices=False)
    dirs_g[L]=Vg[0]; dirs_d[L]=Vd[0]
    print(f"L{L} n={len(grp)} gate top-share {tg:.3f} (random {tg_r:.3f}) | down top-share {td:.3f} (random {td_r:.3f}) | down coherence signed {coh_s:.2f} unsigned {coh_u:.2f} (random ~1) | cos(gate top, D1) {abs(Vg[0]@d1):.2f} cos(gate top,v0) {abs(Vg[0]@v0):.2f}")
for a,b in ((10,11),(11,12),(10,12)):
    print(f"cross-layer |cos| gate-top L{a}-L{b}: {abs(dirs_g[a]@dirs_g[b]):.2f}  down-top: {abs(dirs_d[a]@dirs_d[b]):.2f}")

The 66 neurons write in directions almost orthogonal to D1 (|cos| ≤ 0.18 in every layer). D1 therefore left this channel intact, and its null result says nothing about these neurons.

Their combined writes are large and carry a big share of the math-solve-vs-other difference at the end of the prompt: 70% in L11, 61% in L12, about 30% in L17, L19 and L20. That makes them the main untested candidate for a "task recognized: solve math" mode, which L11h2/h3 then broadcast into the answer.

The causal test (U1) zeroes the down_proj columns of these 66 neurons in their 17 layers, the full-strength removal. Because they are silent during answers, the edit acts essentially only at the end of the prompt.
- **Brake confirmed:** they set a weakened solving mode, so accuracy on DEV[:256] should rise clearly, well beyond the ~3-point standard error.
- **Refuted:** if they are ordinary task-setup units, only the style or opening should change, with accuracy flat or lower.

I will record the exact edit in the notes and save it now.

The U1 edit is saved: 17 down_proj tensors, with the 66 neurons' columns set to zero. The plan is recorded in the notes. I now run the paired generation pass on DEV[:256], the same 256 problems used for E2 and D1, so the results are comparable.

- **Brake:** accuracy rises clearly, by more than about 6 points, which is twice the standard error.
- **Style units:** the answers change in form, with accuracy flat or lower.

U1 changed the answers but not the accuracy: −0.4 ± 2.25 points, with 16 problems going wrong→right and 17 right→wrong. Cut-offs fell from 58 to 37 and answers got shorter. So the 66 end-of-prompt "solve-math" neurons shape length and style, not capability, and the line is closed.

That is now the third perturbation (E2, D1, U1) that changes style or looping while accuracy stays near 22%. The deficit therefore sits in the core computation, not in a mode switch.

Reconsidering the one structural anomaly I found gives a hypothesis I never tested. The ~30–45 rows per layer in L10–12 up_proj carry a huge component along a constant, bias-like input direction (v0). Reading a constant direction is how a bias-free gated MLP builds a threshold, and that is a gate-row role. If those neurons had their gate and up rows swapped, the swap would leave norms intact and look natural at the matrix level. It would also explain why E2, which only removed the v0 part of the "up" rows, slightly hurt instead of helping.

To test this with weight statistics only, I compare, for these neurons and for the bulk:
- the v0 projection of gate rows versus up rows;
- row norms of gate versus up;
- whether the group's "up" rows resemble typical gate rows and vice versa.

A swap is supported if the group's up rows look gate-like and its gate rows look up-like. It is refuted if the group's gate rows also have gate-typical statistics.

The swap hypothesis is refuted. Bulk gate rows do not read v0 either (99th percentile about 0.13–0.15), and the group's gate rows have only small v0 components (median about 0.04). So "gate-like" and "up-like" rows cannot be told apart this way.

The numbers instead show a clean additive signature. The group's up rows look like ordinary up rows (norm about 1.0) plus an added component along v0 of size about 0.84–1.10. The norm arithmetic matches: in L10, √(1.02² + 0.93²) ≈ 1.38 against an observed 1.43; in L12, √(0.98² + 0.84²) ≈ 1.29 against 1.26. The group's gate rows are also 10–20% longer than the bulk (1.03/0.92/1.09 against 0.93/0.85/0.89). That hints that something was added to them too, possibly a shared "trigger" direction that a planted gated circuit would read.

E2 removed only the v0 part, and its −3.1 ± 1.65 is under 2 SE, so it neither confirmed nor cleanly refuted a circuit. I will now check whether the group's gate rows and its down columns share a common direction that random bulk groups of the same size do not:
- the top-singular-value share against bulk;
- cross-layer cosine between those directions;
- cosine with the math direction D1.

A shared extra gate direction or a coherent shared write would mark a planted gated circuit whose real "effect" lies in the down columns. If both look like random bulk, the group is an inert decoy and I close it for good.
